title: Unlicensed Mesh Journalism Networks: Information Outside the Charter
body:
Across the lower residential warrens of Meridian 88 — particularly in the dense stack housing of the Detroit Basin and the industrial-residential mixed zones of the Sarnia Shelf — a parallel information ecosystem operates on peer-to-peer mesh relay protocols that predate the Corporate Expression Protection Ordinance. These networks, collectively referred to by practitioners as 'the Underlayer,' distribute text, audio, and low-resolution video content without CHRB clearance or MNA licensing. The journalists who produce this content — a loose taxonomy that includes former licensed reporters, community investigators, labor organizers with recording equipment, and anonymous whistleblowers — operate under consistent legal exposure. An 'information disturbance' conviction carries a fine of 12,000 credits or citizenship grade reduction of one tier, whichever the adjudicating corporate tribunal determines more appropriate.

The most widely read Underlayer publication is 'The Corrective,' a text-only bulletin distributed three times weekly through encrypted mesh relay. Its editorial collective has maintained operational security for six years, rotating distribution nodes every eleven days and using steganographic embedding in commercial image streams for editorial communications. The Corrective's subject matter focuses primarily on citizenship reclassification patterns, unreported industrial contamination events, and neural interface adverse outcome statistics that the MNA does not carry. Its readership is estimated at between 80,000 and 200,000 distributed across all tiers, though Tier-1 and Tier-2 readership is concentrated among specific professional groups: lawyers, medical personnel, and corporate mid-level employees who seek information not available through licensed channels.

Smaller operations include hyper-local audio bulletins like 'Basin Dispatch' and 'Shelf Watch,' which cover block-level events — evictions, safety incidents, transit disruptions, enforcement actions — with the granularity that licensed media cannot provide because such coverage would require CHRB pre-clearance for any content mentioning corporate enforcement activity. These bulletins are typically produced by single individuals using modified consumer neural interface recording hardware and distributed through physical proximity mesh — the range of a city block — meaning their audiences are simultaneously their neighbors. The intimacy of this distribution model creates a different relationship between producer and reader than licensed broadcast: corrections are immediate, sourcing is personally known, and editorial accountability is social rather than legal.

The corporate enforcement response to Underlayer journalism is not uniform. Low-circulation hyper-local bulletins are generally tolerated as long as they do not cross into 'systemic disturbance' territory — a threshold defined vaguely in the Ordinance and applied inconsistently. Publications that achieve significant cross-sector distribution, particularly those that cover corporate misconduct with documentation, tend to face active suppression: mesh node seizure, source exposure operations, and the use of traffic analysis to identify distribution participants. Several Underlayer journalists have been prosecuted not under the Expression Ordinance but under older fraud and impersonation statutes, a legal strategy that produces longer sentences and avoids the political visibility of expression prosecutions. The journalistic community refers to this practice as 'charge laundering.'
